context: heavy process plant · reheating furnace, rolling stands and cooling bed on deep foundations

brief.intro: New to this project type? A rebar mill heats steel billets to about 1,100 °C in a reheating furnace and passes them through a row of rolling stands that squeeze the glowing bar thinner and longer at every pass, forming the ribs in the last stand. The bar is water-quenched, laid on a long cooling bed, cut to length, bundled and tied. Some plants also have a melt shop — an electric furnace and a caster that make the billets from scrap — which is a larger project again. The mill hall is long, with heavy overhead cranes. Underneath it is a small city of foundations: deep bases for the stands, a scale pit, oil cellars and water channels. Those foundations, the long-lead mill equipment and a big power and water system are what the schedule turns on.

glossary.plain: the square steel bar, typically 130–160 mm, that the mill rolls into rebar.
the furnace that brings billets up to rolling temperature.
a frame holding a pair of grooved rolls that reduce the bar.
rapid water cooling of the bar surface after the last stand, which gives the rebar its strength.
a long rack where bars cool in air and are moved sideways step by step.
a deep pit that collects the cooling water and the iron scale washed off the bar.
the machined plate grouted to the foundation on which a stand is fixed.
a bar that escapes the rolls during rolling — expected during first trials.

must_get_right: Mill foundations are deep, complex and full of cast-in items; they take longer than the building and need complete vendor drawings before the first pour.
Alignment of the mill centre-line is the key quality step — everything else is positioned from it.
Power demand is large (main drives); the grid connection and the substation are schedule items of their own.
Water treatment must be working before any hot rolling; it is often started too late.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant area along the process line and by discipline, with every long-lead machine tracked from order to factory test, shipping and arrival.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for construction; equipment installation may run extended shifts under vendor supervision. Commissioning follows the vendor's programme, and hot commissioning runs continuously once started.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Vendor drawings → deep mill foundations, scale pit and cellars → building and cranes → sole plates and alignment → stands, furnace and cooling bed → hydraulics, water and power → flushing → cold run → furnace heat-up → first hot bar → trials by size. The critical path runs through the foundations and the mill equipment delivery.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The process technology and vendor are fixed before design starts; vendor drawings for foundations arrive on the agreed dates; permanent power and water are available before cold commissioning; raw material for trial production is on site.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy machines need crane access and often must enter before the cladding or a wall is closed. Vendor supervisors are booked for fixed periods. Clean, dry, powered conditions are required before precision equipment is unpacked.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: groundwater in deep pits, late vendor data, late main drives, grid connection, and a long trial period (cobbles, roll changes). Contingency is held before first hot bar.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant area and discipline; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation crews and the vendor supervisors — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
